articles.title: Flock says its cameras make US safer - so why are they being sabotaged?
articles.summary: The AI-powered cameras have been vandalised across the US, as citizens object to the growing surveillance network.
articles.body:
Houston's historic Old Braeswood neighbourhood is affluent and tree-lined.

These are not the kind of streets where you would expect to see coordinated vandalism. Yet here four surveillance cameras were attacked and cut down in the middle of the night.

The metal poles were severed, leaving the distinctive black oval cameras and accompanying solar panels lying on the ground. On some of the cameras was a red sign reading: "Notice. 24/7 video recording".

These cameras are run by a company called Flock Safety and this sabotage, which happened in late July, is a signal of growing concern over the nationwide spread of sophisticated AI-powered surveillance systems. Similar vandalism incidents have occurred in Minnesota, California, and Georgia.

Proponents say they have made communities safer, and helped dramatically increase the rate at which crimes are solved. But recent examples of misuse have led some to worry. Critics say the cameras, which take pictures of the rear of every car that drives past, are overly broad investigative tools that treat civilians like suspects.

They see the little black poles popping up in their neighbourhoods as visible reminders of state power, at a time when public confidence in institutions is historically low and many are concerned about the accelerating pace of technological change and the influence of AI on people's lives.

Founded in 2017, Flock Safety has become one of the country's biggest makers of Automatic Licence Plate Readers (ALPRs). These AI-powered cameras take a picture of the rear of every car that drives past. Footage is retained for a specified amount of time.

But little is known about the extent that Flock is being used - the company does not publish exact data, but says it works with more than 7,000 communities nationwide, and estimates there are approximately 100,000 cameras deployed.

Records obtained by the BBC provide a rare glimpse into the extensive network of cameras and surveillance tech being used in America's fourth largest city, Houston, including the use of controversial facial recognition software powered by artificial intelligence.

Flock is not just selling cameras - it is selling access to a database that can include thousands of cameras from around the country. Older ALPRs did not have this vast network, which is a major selling point for law enforcement.

For example, Houston's METRO Transit Authority owns 35 cameras. But documents show METRO has access to around 20,000 devices in the Flock network - including some as far as Albany County, New York.

And as Flock expands, so too can the scope of investigations. Documents released to the BBC show how the network has grown year on year. In the Cypress-Fairbanks independent school district, a typical licence plate lookup in April 2024 searched around 270 networks of cameras.

By April 2025, the typical search scope had almost doubled to around 500 networks. In April 2026, 20% of searches were conducted across more than 6,000 networks.

Critics in Houston say this national network concerns them more than individual cameras. Christopher Rivera, from the Texas Civil Rights Project, worries that authorities could use "these databases to search our everyday routines, which ultimately scrapes out our routes to work, where our children go to school, and where we worship. And that's very problematic".

There have been recent incidents of privacy breaches that have caught national attention. Last week, a police officer in Kentucky was charged after using the Flock system to track his ex-girlfriend - who filed a protection order - over 2,000 times.

He was caught using Flock's newly mandatory, AI-powered audit tool that flags suspicious use.

Others are concerned about Flock being a way for police to avoid warrants, which are usually required to search a person's property or tap their phone. In 2025, a detective in Johnson County, Texas, searched over 80,000 images to locate a woman suspected of having an abortion. He did not have a warrant.

CCTV cameras, licence plate readers, and surveillance are not new. But the scale of Flock's network and the integration of AI in modern surveillance tech is a recent development and it's turned Flock into a household name. Americans who otherwise ignored the cameras in their cities have started to notice, and tune in to the capabilities of the technology around them.

With AI, unlike older licence-plate readers, law enforcement can search surveillance footage with a string of words like "Caucasian man, blue shirt" - not just a licence-plate image.

One thing Flock does not use is facial recognition. But that doesn't mean police departments are avoiding that tech. Critics say it violates human rights, is susceptible to misidentifying innocent people, and can be biased against minorities.

The BBC has received documents revealing that Harris County Sheriff's Office, which covers Houston, uses other facial recognition technology, Clearview AI. The tool includes a database of over 70 billion images, many of which were scraped from public internet sources including social media. The documents, including purchase orders and a License Agreement, show that the county's Clearview AI contract currently runs through to March 2027.

Several European countries have issued the company with data protection fines, including a £7.5m penalty from the UK's Information Commissioner.

Harris County Sheriff's Office use of this facial recognition technology has not been reported before. The office did not respond to requests for comment.

Police say surveillance technology like this, including Flock cameras, is important for fighting crime.

"It's a very good tool," says Chief Ray Schultz of the Memorial Villages Police Department - a small jurisdiction within Houston. "It makes the community safer." Before purchasing a Flock ALPR, his department would recover an average of three stolen cars a year. Now, this figure is 45, Schultz says.

Some crimes solved in recent years would have been "impossible" without Flock, he adds. Last month, Schultz used the tool to find an elderly woman with dementia who had driven 60 miles from Galveston to Houston and had got lost. "We were able to find her and reunite her with her family."

Schultz says that it is important for agencies to have strong policies governing ALPR use and officers that misuse the system should be held accountable.

"But don't throw out a tool that is valuable, that can help recover a missing child."

Jasmine Khadem Gonzalez, an immigrant rights organiser, is worried that law enforcement might "use [the Flock] database to tell ICE where somebody is".

The federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency does not have a contract with Flock directly. However, there have been reports of police officers citing "immigration" or "ice" as a reason for searching a licence plate.

Jessie, an immigrant from Central America, noticed a Flock camera outside her house last month. She asked the BBC to not use her real name out of fear it could impact a pending case to extend her green card.

"It makes me feel as if I'm being stalked," she says.

In response, she's changed her commute to work: "I try to take different routes every day so there's not a pattern."

But whether individual law enforcement agencies share info with the federal government is unclear. Federal immigration enforcement cannot access Flock data directly, Flock's CEO says. But some police departments have standing agreements with federal immigration enforcement to work together.

In Harris County, a proposed Flock contract amendment initially included the explicit authorisation to share camera data with federal law enforcement, but this provision was later removed after push-back from campaigners.

Some jurisdictions have opted not to renew contracts with Flock as a result of these concerns, including large metropolitan areas like Los Angeles, Seattle, and Austin, Texas.

In total, over 200 communities have cancelled or not renewed their contracts since 2021 - including 90 in the month of August alone - according to advocacy group Secure Justice . Their reasons for cancelling may include cost and concerns about data privacy.

Nationally, lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have suggested there ought to be guardrails and several candidates have made it a campaign issue for the upcoming midterms. Republican Congressman Keith Self has proposed legislation that would require federal agencies to get warrants before accessing Flock data.

The company itself has also amended some of its policies, such as requiring mandatory audits, and reducing the default period that data stays on a server from 30 days to 7 days, unless flagged as part of an investigation. But individual agencies can choose to retain data for much longer.

Flock Safety's CEO and founder, Garrett Langley, told the BBC it's up to individual cities to decide how long to store data, and what information to share with whom.

"I don't think a technology company should be making decisions like that," he says.

"As long as it's a lawful investigation, we are not going to tell cities what laws they should or should not enforce."

Flock is a safety, not surveillance, company, Langley says. Yet three patents filed between 2020 and 2025 have the word "surveillance" in the title.

He boasts that the tech helped solve "about a million crimes" and helped find over 10,000 missing people.

"The debate of how we build a society where safety and privacy coexist" is worth having, he says, but the ongoing vandalism is "disappointing".

But there is nothing Flock or law enforcement could say to make Jessie feel at ease with this technology, she says. "I just don't trust that they're doing it to keep us safe."

articles.title: From cockroach milk to stepping on snakes, Ig Nobel awards celebrates science at its oddest
articles.summary: Cockroach milk, kissing evolution and the underwear soil test were among the unusual real studies honored at the Ig Nobel ceremony in Zurich.
articles.body: A motley crew of scientists was honored this week for its unusual contributions, which included studying cockroach milk, the evolutionary history of kissing and testing soil health by using underwear. The satirical Ig Nobel ceremony, which honors unusual but real studies, took place in Zurich Thursday and was presented by the digital magazine, the Annals of Improbable Research. The awards, which were founded in 1991, took place outside the U.S. for the first time this year over the concern that the honorees wouldn’t be able to get a visa. Other winners included researchers who found upper-class people were more likely to engage in unethical behavior, such as stealing candy from a baby, a study on proper nose blowing and gently stepping on snakes to see what provokes them into biting people. WASHINGTON HOMEOWNER HEARS MYSTERIOUS BANGING CALLS 911 BEFORE POLICE FIND GROWLING BOBCAT AT TOP OF STAIRS "The general pattern seems to be that, with wealth and rising power, you become less engaged with the needs of others and less burdened by the needs of social relationships," Dr. Paul Piff, a social psychologist at the University of California, Irvine said, according to the Guardian. "Taking candy from children might be the least of our worries, but it’s emblematic of the tendency to prioritize one’s own needs over those of others." The final four honorees included those studying the power of having mutual enemies, attempts at a splash-free urinal, using dead mosquitos for 3D printing and research that found parents love the smell of their newborn babies but not teenage children. In case you’re wondering, the team studying the history of kissing has defined it as "a non-agonistic interaction involving directed, intraspecific, oral-oral contact with some movement of the lips/mouthparts and no food transfer." Romantic. COUPLE PUBLICLY CANED AFTER ALLEGED TIKTOK KISS SPARKS OUTRAGE IN INDONESIA "Next time you kiss someone, you can think, 'This is a 21.5 million-year-old tradition that I'm honoring here," evolutionary biologist Matilda Brindle of the University of Oxford said, according to NPR. "It's not just a modern human behavior. It's really ancestral.' And to us, that suggests that it probably has quite a useful evolutionary function." Brindle said her team believes that Neanderthals not only kissed each other. They may have also kissed early humans. CAVE DISCOVERY PUSHES BACK EVIDENCE OF HUMAN ANCESTORS USING FIRE TO 1.79M YEARS AGO All the honorees receive a trophy that looks like a cross between a mushroom and a human foot while the audience throws paper airplanes at them. articles.title: Fresh FIR against Swatantra Bhardwaj under POCSO Act: How ‘influencer’ tried to evade police in UP
articles.summary: BULANDSHAHR: Swatantra Bhardwaj, a social media “influencer” accused of assaulting the father of a student activist during CJP’s July protest at Delhi.
articles.body: BULANDSHAHR: Swatantra Bhardwaj, a social media “influencer” accused of assaulting the father of a student activist during CJP’s July protest at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar, was “apprehended and detained” in UP’s Bulandshahr Friday, sources told TOI.The reported action against Bhardwaj came after CJP co-conveners Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, along with supporters and some politicians, reached Parliament Street police station in Delhi, demanding stricter sections in the assault case.In a late development, a fresh FIR was registered against Bhardwaj under Pocso Act. Relevant sections of SC/ST Act were also added to earlier FIR, sources said.Bhardwaj had publicly said he had “cracked the skull” of the minor activist’s father during the protest, and bragged about being out of jail due to his ‘political connections’.Bhardwaj arrived in Bulandshahr to evade arrest, stayed with a localAccording to local residents in Bulandshahr who spoke to TOI, Bhardwaj arrived in the UP district early Friday, allegedly to evade arrest, and took shelter at the home of a local family in Naithla village. While there, he interacted with a few journalists and reportedly reiterated his claims about the “assault” during the CJP protest.According to CJP representatives Friday, Delhi Police had assured that Bhardwaj “will be arrested within 72 hours”.Bhardwaj was staying at the house of Harishankar Sharma, a Naithla resident who works as a cab driver in the Delhi-NCR region. Sharma told TOI that he had met Bhardwaj during a previous journey.“Bhardwaj called me and said he wanted to come to my house to meet me. He arrived early in the morning along with another man. Initially, I did not suspect anything. But when media persons started arriving at my village, I sensed something was wrong,” Sharma said.Sharma added that Bhardwaj later asked if he could borrow a motorcycle, saying he would return “within five minutes”. “Then I came to know that Delhi Police had detained him. It was only after that I learnt that he was wanted in a criminal case in the national capital. I still do not know much about the case,” Sharma said.Sharma later told ANI: “He was with me until 2 pm. The crime branch came from Delhi and took him away. They just came and said, ‘We’re from the crime branch; Swatantra, come with us,’ and took him along...”Shamshuddin Saifi, another local resident, claimed, “Some villagers became suspicious after spotting a car with three men in plainclothes. When we questioned the occupants, they said they were from the police... Later, we heard that Bhardwaj had been picked up from Dhameda Nara village in Bulandshahr.”Sikandrabad circle officer (CO) Deepak Kumar said the local police came to know about Bhardwaj’s presence via WhatsApp media groups. “We immediately sent a local police team to the area, but by the time the team reached, he had left that place,” the CO said, adding that Delhi Police officers did not record their arrival at the local police station.Originally from Bihar, Bhardwaj, who is in his early 20s, currently lives in Delhi, where he is pursuing his studies and preparing for govt service examinations, according to information on his social media profiles. His online accounts suggest he completed his schooling in Patna before relocating to Delhi. Bhardwaj describes himself as a “Sanatani Yoddha” and has built a sizeable following on social media, where he has posted several provocative videos and hate content.The minor activist alleged that she faced verbal abuse and rape threats after complaining about the assault on her father and filing an FIR. “It was hard to even step out. articles.title: Why are European countries moving their gold out of North America?
articles.summary: The Netherlands has relocated 86 tonnes of the shiny stuff - what's going on?
articles.body:
When the central bank of the Netherlands confirmed this week that it had moved tonnes of the country's gold out of North America, it said the relocation would make it "better prepared for severe crises".

Some 86 tonnes from the combined total of about 313 tonnes held in the US and Canada were relocated to London "in view of increasing geopolitical unrest", it said, so the shiny stuff could be "readily available for use in a crisis situation".

Questions were bound to follow. Why were the Dutch doing this? Were they anticipating some major economic shock on the horizon?

It seems not, but the move was clearly in response to the unstable and uncertain state the world finds itself in, with trade and military wars prompting countries to take precautions and hold their gold closer to home.

Earlier this year, France announced it had removed its gold reserves from the US to home shores. Meanwhile, Germany's Bundesbank transferred more than 216 tonnes of the metal from storage locations abroad - 111 tonnes from New York and 105 tonnes from Paris - over a few years ending in 2016.

It is a strategy which has played out before in times of global instability. "Some European central banks moved part of their gold holdings to New York during the Cold War," said research analysts Lina Thomas and Daan Struyven of Goldman Sachs.

Joseph Cavatoni, senior market strategist at the World Gold Council, told the BBC while wars and trade tensions were "playing into some of these decisions", it didn't "top the list" of motivating factors.

Inflation, interest rates and just having gold in a place where it can be traded quickly also played a role.

"I don't get a sense that there's an impending doom," Cavatoni said, "but what I do think is people are being better educated around how to manage their reserve assets, growing their reserve assets, and actually thinking more effectively around how to make the most of those assets."

De Nederlandsche Bank said the gold removed from the US and Canada between March and August this year was now being held in the vaults of the Bank of England.

"We expect that we will never need to use them, but we do need to strengthen our resilience and preparedness," said the governor of the Dutch central bank, Olaf Sleijpen.

London was seen as the best choice due its position in the world as a major trading centre. If you want to be able to buy or sell gold fast in a crisis, London is the place to be, which makes the Bank of England a popular storage spot.

The Bank is one of the largest custodians of gold in the world. Underneath the 300-year-old institution in central London sits about 400,000 bars worth more than £200bn.

According to industry surveys by the World Gold Council, the Bank of England remains the most popular vaulting location, but central banks are increasingly diversifying where they store the precious metal.

Where to store your country's gold is "increasingly top of mind for reserve managers", according to Thomas and Struyven of Goldman Sachs.

In the modern world, there are many ways to shift your treasure around. The Dutch sold about 59 tonnes in New York and then bought more stocks in London, meaning that amount didn't need to be hauled across the Atlantic.

But more than 27 tonnes were "physically transferred" from the US and Canada to the Dutch town of Zeist. A similar quantity was also sent from Zeist to London.

Companies that perform such services are tight-lipped on how operations are carried out, but it's fair to say the security measures and planning are extensive to avoid the risk of a real-life Italian Job.

Cavatoni, of the World Gold Council, said one standard approach to move gold stocks was to sell the commodity in one place and buy it in another. "Let's say I want my gold in New York and I have it in London. I could sell it in London, buy it in New York, same day, same time, effectively book transfer without actually having to put it on any other logistical change."

There are only a few select companies which handle gold shipments across borders, one of which is Brink's Global Services, who told the BBC it had seen "increased demand" from the likes of central banks in recent times.

"Heightened geopolitical and economic uncertainty, along with gold's growing role as a strategic reserve asset, appear to be contributing to this trend," said Nader Antar, Brink's executive vice president.

The reason gold storage is such a topic in the minds of central banks is because they have been increasingly buying the stuff. But storing it at home comes at a cost, said Thomas and Struyven of Goldman Sachs.

"Domestic storage requires investment in physical security, audit infrastructure, and insurance; costs that can be disproportionate for smaller central banks," they said.

Over the past four years, central banks have accumulated an annual average of 1,000 tonnes of gold, up significantly from the 500 tonnes average over the preceding decade, according to the World Gold Council.

The trend stretches back to the global financial crisis. And that is only expected to go up in the next year.

Gold has been having a moment in recent years. Its price has surged to hit a series of record highs, passing $5,000 an ounce in January.

There are several reasons behind its value jumping, but a major factor has been the precious metal's position in the human psyche as a so-called safe haven asset, to invest during periods of financial and geopolitical turmoil caused through trade and military wars.

Inflation and interest rates also influence gold's popularity. Due to the commodity's scarcity and the value placed on it across thousands of years, it is somewhat resistant against rising prices, and so is seen as a good investment.

"Over the past half-century, gold prices have risen much faster than the Consumer Price Index (CPI) - the most closely watched measure of inflation," according to investment bank Charles Schwab.

While the price of gold has fallen from the record high seen early this year, it still remains at a high level historically.

According to researchers at Goldman, the price is forecast to rise to $4,900 (£3,624) per troy ounce by the end of 2026, $300 more than it was in August.

The demand for gold from central banks is one key reason why prices are surging, according to Thomas and Struyven.

articles.title: Ecuador defends US sinking of vessels as joint anti-drug operation
articles.summary: Relatives of detained crew say US forces acted without evidence, claiming the men were fishermen, not smugglers.
articles.body:
Ecuador has defended a US operation this week that sank three vessels accused of sustaining drug-trafficking operations in the Eastern Pacific.

Ecuador’s government said on Friday the interception and sinking of the Ecuadorian vessels were part of joint investigations ⁠with Washington targeting drug-smuggling activities linked to criminal gangs.

Ecuadorian Interior Minister John Reimberg told broadcaster Teleamazonas the vessels were refueling points for speedboats that move drugs north towards Mexico and the United States.

“This is ⁠work carried out through international cooperation,” Reimberg said.

The US Southern Command (SOUTHCOM) reiterated Reimberg’s claim, saying it “successfully interdicted a vessel operating as a floating refueling station in support of illicit at-sea drug trafficking operations”, linked to the Los Choneros gang.

“Individuals removed from the vessel will be safely transferred to Ecuadorian authorities. Once cleared, U.S. forces sank the vessel,” SOUTHCOM posted on X on Thursday.

A video accompanying SOUTHCOM’s post showed US forces approaching and boarding a vessel before it was blown up at sea. The time and location of the video have not been independently verified.

Relatives of some crew members accused the US military of acting without evidence and said the men on the boats were fishermen. The wife of one crew member told the Reuters news agency in a phone interview that the men had been fishing when US forces boarded and that no drugs were found. Her account has not been independently verified.

The Ecuadorian navy said that it received 28 crew members from that vessel and another boat that was sunk on Wednesday and that they arrived in Manta, the country’s main fishing port, on board a local coastguard vessel.

On Friday, a group of people waited for news of their relatives who, they said, were traveling on the boats targeted in the past two days, the AFP news agency reported.

The incidents are the latest in the Trump administration’s campaign against maritime drug trafficking that has drawn concern in Latin America over the use of air attacks and lethal force on international waters.

SOUTHCOM confirmed a previous attack on a “low-profile” vessel that killed two people on August 23. Another US strike killed four people two days later. No victims were identified in either attack.

Trump has claimed the US is in a “non-international armed conflict” with drug-trafficking organisations in an unreleased memo obtained by US media.

articles.body: At least 10 people were killed and more than 60 injured on Friday after an explosion struck a military base in Bolivia, local health director Rita Nebraska told television station Noticias Bolivision.The explosion took place at about 2.30 pm local time at a military complex in Viacha, around 30 km (19 miles) from La Paz. The blast hit an area where pyrotechnic material was being stored, authorities said.Officials have yet to determine what triggered the explosion, but said it came from a stockpile of fireworks held by the country's defence ministry, reported Reuters.Nebraska said the death toll could be as high as 15, with 62 people reported injured. Fourteen injured people were taken to hospitals in La Paz, including a girl who suffered third-degree burns.Police said more than 50 people were injured and that the explosion caused damage to dozens of homes in the surrounding area. Most of the reported damage was caused by windows being shattered by the force of the blast.Emergency services rushed to the military complex, with ambulances, medical teams and police personnel deployed to assess the scene and transport the wounded to medical facilities.Authorities also warned residents to keep away from the site. Nebraska said firefighters had detected a remaining heat source at the complex, raising concerns that it could trigger another explosion. articles.title: Jay-Z: Stars join US rapper at long-awaited UK show
articles.summary: The US rapper rolled back the years for more than two hours at the first of his two shows in London.
articles.body:
Jay-Z's first headline solo show in the UK in more than a decade saw him celebrate hip-hop culture alongside a host of special guests, including Lauryn Hill, Wyclef Jean and Giggs.

The US rap superstar rolled back the years for more than two hours - playing hits like 99 Problems, Empire State of Mind and Dead Presidents - as he took to the stage at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium on Friday night for the first of two shows in London this weekend.

The run is part of his Jay-Z 30 tour, which is marking the 30th anniversary of his debut album, Reasonable Doubt, and his culture-shaping career that followed.

Fans of his wife Beyoncé had hoped she would join him on stage, like she did at two of his three New York shows this summer, as she was also celebrating her 45th birthday on Friday.

Toward the end of the show, Jay-Z mentioned it was a "young lady's birthday", sending the crowd into a frenzy, but he joked that he couldn't make her perform on her big day.

Instead he asked the crowd to join him in singing Happy Birthday to the US superstar, who was sat in a private box, while sparkler-like fireworks erupted in the sky.

The show's opening set the tone for the star-studded evening to follow, as British actor Sir Idris Elba kicked things off by performing the intro track to his 2007 album, American Gangster.

As Jay-Z took to the stage, he recalled coming to London in 1989 with his mentor Jaz-O and seeing "what was possible" and it became a "special" place in his career.

His return to the capital this time round was explosive, with the rapper rattling through a string of hits like Izzo (H.O.V.A.), On To The Next One and Song Cry.

Throughout the show, vintage video clips and moments from his early career played across a massive LED screen, while an orchestra and a few guitarists accompanied him on stage.

There was no sign of Rihanna or Alicia Keys, who both made appearances during the New York run for their collaboration tracks, but the crowd made up for their absence by chanting back their lyrics during Run This Town and Empire State of Mind.

Jay-Z also took a moment to thank his fans who have been there from the beginning, telling them that "music saved my life".

His reflective mood continued as he performed Hard Knock Life (Ghetto Anthem) and Where I'm From, which explores his upbringing in the Marcy housing projects in Brooklyn, New York.

He cranked the energy back up for his 2011 hit No Church in the Wild, which was amplified by firey pyrotechnics that radiated heat through the stadium.

Originally a collaboration with controversial rapper Ye, also known as Kanye West, Jay-Z left his voice in for the chorus but cut his verses out.

US DJ Khaled had a brief moment on stage while Jay-Z changed, but it was the appearance of London-born rapper Giggs which got the crowd erupting.

He appeared overwhelmed at one stage, his hand clutching his face, as he took in the packed crowd while performing his track Talkin Da Hardest alongside Jay-Z.

The surprise guests didn't stop there, as Lauryn Hill and Wyclef Jean from the 90s American hip-hop collective Fugees reunited to perform their hit tracks Ready or Not, Killing Me Softly With His Song and Fu-Gee-La.

It was a full circle moment for both them and Jay-Z as he recalled supporting them on their European tour.

The US rap superstar closed out the night with rousing renditions of Public Service Announcement (Interlude) and Numb/Encore, hailing it as a "legendary night" that he would "never forget".

The crowd appeared to agree as thousands praised him by holding up his famous diamond hand gesture.

Fans had travelled from across the UK and the world to see the rapper, including Prince Dean Sithole, who hailed Jay-Z as one of his role models.

"I think he's very impacting, especially for us black people because we don't get a lot of recognition," the 19-year-old from Leeds told BBC Newsbeat.

"Seeing him today shows that dreams are possible and you can be that person that you want to be."

Jay-Z, real name Shawn Carter, broke through with his 1996 debut album, but it was his third record, Vol. 2: Hard Knock Life, in 1998 which landed him the top spot in the US charts for the first time and a best rap album Grammy.

He went on to establish himself as one of the most influential figures in hip-hop, releasing 13 solo studio albums and several collaboration records, which have secured him 25 Grammy Awards.

He was also the first rapper inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 2017, as well being inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2021.

Over the years, he has also become one of the most prominent music mogul's in the world, with his company Roc Nation representing a host of top talent and, in recent years, it has been behind the Super Bowl half-time show.

In 2019, he was declared hip-hop's first billionaire by Forbes, having built an empire based on music, property, fashion and investments alongside his wife Beyoncé.

The power couple have three children, daughter Blue Ivy, 14, and 9-year-old twins, Rumi and Sir.

articles.title: A bigger Africa & a smaller Europe: What changes in new UN-backed world map
articles.summary: Rest of World News: The United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) on Friday endorsed a new world map that more accurately reflects Africa’s actual size, marking the culminat.
articles.body: The United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) on Friday endorsed a new world map that more accurately reflects Africa’s actual size, marking the culmination of a Togo-led campaign backed by the African Union and various advocacy groups.The UNGA adopted a resolution titled “Correct The Map”, with 164 member states voting in favour. The United States was the only country to vote against the resolution, while six countries — Serbia, Estonia, Georgia, Lithuania, Moldova and Ukraine — abstained.The campaign urged governments and institutions worldwide to move away from the traditional Mercator projection, which has been widely used since the 16th century, and adopt the Equal Earth projection. Advocates and geographers say the Equal Earth map provides a more accurate representation of the relative size and proportions of continents.Under the Mercator projection, Greenland appears roughly comparable in size to Africa, despite being far smaller. The Equal Earth projection, by contrast, depicts continents in more accurate proportions, showing Africa as about 14 times larger than Greenland.However, the resolution does not prohibit the use of the Mercator projection or mandate its replacement. According to a UN report, it simply encourages governments and institutions to consider using the Equal Earth projection instead.“Maps shape our understanding of the world,” Togo’s foreign minister Robert Dussey was quoted by the UN as saying ahead of the vote. “They guide education, nourish the imagination, and influence collective perceptions.”Africa No Filter, one of the leading groups behind the campaign to promote the new map, welcomed the resolution and called for more widespread use of accurate maps.“We want to see accurate maps in schools, textbooks, newsrooms, businesses and on the digital platforms billions of people use every day,” the organisation said.Several countries also welcomed the resolution and backed greater adoption of the Equal Earth projection. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said on X following the vote: “Changing the map obviously doesn’t change the world. But correcting a representation that distorts it is already an act of truth.”The Mercator projection was developed by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator to assist European navigators at sea. However, critics argue that the projection significantly distorts the size of landmasses, making regions closer to the poles, such as North America and Greenland, appear much larger while making Africa and South America appear smaller.Introduced in 2018, the Equal Earth projection takes the Earth’s curvature into account and presents continents in proportions that more closely reflect their actual size. In it, Europe appears to shrink, Brazil balloons, and Greenland dramatically diminishes. Africa appears much larger in comparison.(With AP inputs)Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Burning Man attendee dies at festival
articles.summary: A man died while attending the annual Burning Man festival in the Nevada desert this week, the festival said Thursday.
articles.body: A man died while attending the annual Burning Man festival in the Nevada desert this week, the festival said Thursday. The festivalgoer was described as being in his mid-50s and had a medical emergency at the event, it said in a statement. He “immediately received lifesaving measures, and was transported to the onsite center for emergency care where he was pronounced deceased,” the festival said. The man’s identity was being withheld until family could be notified, it said. The Pershing County Sheriff’s Office, which doubles as the region’s medical examiner, did not immediately respond to a request for information. The cause and manner of death have not been released. “The safety and well-being of our community and staff remain our highest priority,” the festival said. The death came as the festival endured another year with weather woes, including rain on Friday that temporarily closed a main gate to festival grounds known as Black Rock City. By 6 p.m. on Friday the gate was reopened, organizers said in a discussion board post. The National Weather Service called for blowing dust early Friday evening and a 20% chance of rain on Sunday for nearby Gerlach, Nevada, a community of 58 people about 100 miles north of Reno. The festival, with a capacity of 80,000 people, also was hit with mud and rain in 2023 as many attendees were trapped on its grounds, where vehicle traffic was temporarily limited and some hiked in the mud to nearby towns. Burning Man kicked off Aug. 30 and is scheduled through Sept. 7. The post-hippie, psychedelic festival of DJ-performed music, art installations, and temporary communal living takes place each year on 3,400 acres of dry lake and desert land in northern Nevada run by the U.S. Bureau of Land Management. It’s celebrating its 40th year, with its roots in a 1986 gathering on San Francisco’s Baker Beach said to have drawn roughly 20 people for the planned, bonfire burning of an 8-foot wooden structure known as “the Man.”

articles.title: Tate brothers charged with further trafficking and sex crimes in Romania
articles.summary: Andrew and Tristan Tate are currently in a Miami jail fighting extradition to the UK over separate charges and deny all the allegations.
articles.body:
Romanian prosecutors have charged social media influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate with further sex crimes.

They are accused of making more than $1.2m (£888,000) by coercing a girl to do sex acts on video chats, according to the Romanian Directorate for Investigating Crime and Terrorism (DIICOT).

Andrew, 39, is charged with trafficking minors, money laundering and sex with a minor. Tristan, 38, is charged with complicity in trafficking in minors and money laundering.

The Tates - currently in a Miami jail fighting extradition to the UK over separate charges - deny all the allegations.

Will the Tate brothers be extradited from the US to the UK?

The brothers - former kickboxers with dual US and British citizenship - have been under criminal investigation in Romania since December 2022.

They have been mainly based there since 2017, drawing a large social media audience - many of them young men - through misogynistic messages and images of a luxury lifestyle.

Many of the new charges centre on a vulnerable woman investigators allege was recruited by Tristan when she was 15.

She is alleged to have been sheltered in a building in Luton, Bedfordshire, for sexual exploitation by Andrew.

DIICOT investigators allege Andrew controlled her through surveillance and physical aggression and coerced her to perform sex acts on video chats for his financial gain.

He is also accused of moving her to Romania to carry on exploiting her in two of his homes.

Andrew is separately charged with having sex with a minor, who was 15, in Romania.

Prosecutors have also requested four of the brothers' luxury cars worth £710,000 are confiscated. They believe money was laundered through their purchase.

It is not yet clear if DIICOT will seek their extradition from the US, and the indictment has to be examined by a judge before any trial can open.

The Tates have denied all the allegations and say their online personas are not their real personalities.

Their lawyer Eugen Constantin Vidineac said: "Today's decision by DIICOT does not determine guilt and it should not be presented as though it does. It represents the prosecution's latest attempt to bring this case before a court following the failure of its previous indictment to proceed to trial.

"The history of these proceedings matters. The previous indictment was subjected to judicial scrutiny and the court identified significant irregularities which prevented the case from moving forward to trial.

"DIICOT has now chosen to file a new indictment. We will examine every aspect of it with the same level of scrutiny and we will challenge any evidential, procedural or legal deficiencies through the appropriate judicial process.

"Our clients continue to reject the allegations against them. They have the right to the presumption of innocence, the right to properly examine the evidence relied upon against them and the right to mount an effective defence."

articles.title: ‘To challenge deadly blockade’: New flotilla mission sets sail for Gaza
articles.summary: Human rights advocates call for diplomatic measures to guarantee flotilla safety and end Israel’s deadly Gaza blockade.
articles.body:
The Freedom Flotilla Coalition (FFC) has announced that a new international mission is under way, with vessels stopping at European ports ahead of its attempt to reach Gaza’s shores in October.

The coalition said in a statement that the mission to “challenge Israel’s illegal and deadly blockade of Gaza” would go ahead despite the violence Israeli forces inflicted on flotilla volunteers and activists, such as documented cases of severe beatings, repeated tasering and sexual assault.

It added that “action is needed now more than ever as much of the world has moved on from Gaza” since the announcement of a ceasefire in October 2025.

According to the statement, two vessels have already set out. Handala II sailed around Scandinavia in June and July, stopping in Norway, Sweden and Denmark, while the ship Kate departed Bristol, UK, earlier this month and has since called at ports in Ireland, Germany and France.

Stops in Spain, Portugal and Italy are planned before the flotilla continues towards Gaza, the mission added.

“The Freedom Flotilla sails again because our governments continue to fail to uphold their obligations,” said Zohar Chamberlain Regev, an FFC Steering Committee member.

“At every port, we will carry the demand that Palestinians be free to live with dignity,” he added.

Human rights advocates, peace activists, elected representatives, journalists, medical professionals and advocates for Palestinian rights have joined the new flotilla.

The coalition is calling on governments to guarantee safe passage for the flotilla, press Israel to end its obstruction of food, water and medicine into Gaza, declare that any attack or seizure of the vessels will trigger diplomatic consequences and use diplomatic and economic measures to end the blockade.

“We know that sailing toward Gaza carries serious risks,” said Edward Digilio, an engineer from Maryland taking part in the mission. “But silence and inaction carry a much greater cost for Palestinians and the world.”

Pattern of Israeli interception and abuse

The coalition traces its roots to 2010, when Israeli forces killed 10 activists on board the Mavi Marmara during a flotilla attempt, and to the Free Gaza Movement’s first voyages in 2008.

Israeli forces intercepted the Global Sumud Flotilla twice within the past year, detaining more than 450 participants in October 2025 — including South African author Zukiswa Wanner and Nelson Mandela’s grandson, Mandla Mandela — and about 175 more in April 2026.

Amnesty International said it documented sleep deprivation, denial of water and medical care, and other ill-treatment of activists held by Israel after intercepting and storming the ships.

Two activists, Thiago Avila and Saif Abukeshek, were held incommunicado for days in April this year and had their detention extended partly on secret evidence before being deported.

The mission joins many other aid groups who have described Gaza’s humanitarian situation as reaching crisis levels despite the ceasefire.

UNICEF estimates that more than 82 percent of families remain water insecure and roughly 90 percent of water and sanitation infrastructure is destroyed.

Israel has continued to target hospitals, aid warehouses and medical supply sites in Gaza in recent weeks.

Gaza’s Health Ministry has recorded more than 1,300 deaths from Israeli fire since the truce took effect in October, alongside thousands still missing or believed trapped under rubble.

articles.title: At least two dead in blast at Bolivia military barracks
articles.summary: Authorities fear the death toll in Viacha will rise and warn people to stay away from the barracks due to a risk of further explosions.
articles.body:
At least two people have been killed after an explosion at a military barracks in Bolivia but authorities fear the toll could be higher.

Bolivian Defence Minister Ernesto Justiniano said at least 58 people had been injured when "pyrotechnic material" detonated at the barracks, where an artillery regiment is stationed, about 14:30 (18:30 GMT) on Friday.

Health official Rita Nebraska told local television between 10 and 15 people were believed to have died in the incident in Viacha, about 30km (19 miles) from La Paz, according to Reuters.

Police said dozens of homes had been damaged - largely windows shattered in the blast - and emergency workers are searching the rubble.

Nebraska said there was a risk of further explosion and urged people to stay at least 150m away from the military base.

Police spokesman Roger Roca told AFP news agency that fireworks had been stored at the barracks, and the cause of the blast remained under investigation.

Viacha's authorities have declared three days of mourning.

images.caption: The explosion happened at a barracks in Viacha, about 30km from La Paz

articles.title: After Pretoria peace deal, old enemies in Ethiopia’s Tigray find new ground
articles.summary: The 2022 peace deal ended the war but left key disputes unresolved, giving the TPLF room to regroup as tensions return.
articles.body:
Addis Ababa, Ethiopia – When Ethiopia’s federal government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) signed the Pretoria Agreement in November 2022, it was meant to end two years of devastating war.

The agreement called for a permanent cessation of hostilities, the disarmament, demobilisation and reintegration of Tigrayan forces, political dialogue and the return of displaced people. Article 7 also required the TPLF to refrain from conscription, training, deployment and mobilisation of military forces, as well as preparations for renewed conflict.

Nearly four years later, the large-scale war has ended, but many of the disputes that fuelled it remain unresolved.

More significantly, the period since 2024 has seen the TPLF reposition itself politically and organisationally while retaining military leverage and developing new relationships.

The sequence is striking: TPLF contacts with Eritrean officials, including reported meetings in Dubai and Zalambessa; a renewed struggle over political control in Tigray; reports of recruitment and mobilisation; new clashes involving Tigrayan forces; and the emergence of Tsimdo, a loose convergence of groups opposed to the federal government.

Taken together, the developments raise a question over whether Pretoria became less a completed transition to peace than a period in which the TPLF could regroup and reposition itself while the underlying conflict remained unresolved.

There is no evidence that the TPLF entered the agreement with a predetermined plan to use it as a tactical pause. But the events since 2024 suggest that the movement has retained an organisational and security role that Pretoria was supposed to diminish.

Article 6 established the process for disarming, demobilising and reintegrating TPLF fighters. Tigrayan forces handed over heavy weapons after the agreement, and thousands of former combatants have entered demobilisation programmes.

But the process did not fully dismantle the region’s military structures.

In 2026, reports emerged of renewed recruitment and forced mobilisation in Tigray. If confirmed, such activity would go beyond the incomplete implementation of the disarmament, demobilisation and reintegration (DDR) process and directly challenge Article 7’s ban on conscription and mobilisation.

The distinction between organised mobilisation and the views of Tigray’s civilian population is important.

There is no basis for assuming that Tigrayans as a whole support a return to war. Many are still living with the consequences of the last conflict.

A civilian source in Tigray, who spoke to Al Jazeera on condition of anonymity, said: “The people of Tigray want peace; we don’t want a second war.”

For those civilians, reports of recruitment carry a simple implication: the possibility of being pulled back into a conflict they believed had ended.

The change was not only in the military.

From 2024, the TPLF was increasingly consumed by an internal struggle over its direction after the war. The internal meetings and political manoeuvring formed part of a wider contest over the movement’s future.

The struggle eventually reached Tigray’s political institutions.

Getachew Reda was removed as head of the interim administration in 2025 and replaced by Lieutenant General Tadesse Werede.

Then, in May 2026, the Tigray regional council was reinstated and elected Debretsion Gebremichael as president, strengthening the position of the faction around him.

The developments showed that the TPLF remained a powerful political force in Tigray. Instead of a settled post-war political order emerging, the region was again caught in a struggle over authority while the security question remained unresolved.

When did politics turn back into fighting?

By early 2026, political tensions were accompanied by military developments.

Tigray Defence Forces-aligned troops crossed the Tekeze River into the disputed Tselemt district in January and clashed with Ethiopian federal forces. Later, TDF-aligned fighters took control of Alamata and Korem after a federal command post withdrew.

By August, fighting had again broken out in western Tigray near the Sudanese border, in another serious breach of the peace agreement.

The federal government and the TPLF blamed each other for the escalation, while responsibility for initiating the clashes remained disputed.

But the renewed fighting demonstrated that organised armed forces were still capable of mobilising and contesting territory.

The incomplete disarmament has therefore become more consequential as the political disputes left unresolved by Pretoria have begun to coincide with renewed military activity.

Why are former enemies finding common ground?

The repositioning has extended beyond Tigray.

Eritrea and the TPLF fought a devastating border war from 1998 to 2000. Eritrean forces later fought alongside Ethiopia’s federal government against the TPLF during the 2020-22 Tigray war.

Yet the post-Pretoria period has brought reports of closer contacts between Eritrea and elements of the TPLF.

Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of supporting the TPLF and using it as a proxy. Eritrea rejects that characterisation.

A broader realignment is reflected in the emergence of Tsimdo, a loose convergence of groups opposed to the federal government.

Recent reporting has identified cooperation involving the TPLF, Fano, the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA) and other armed groups. Fano leader Zemene Kassie has confirmed the existence of such a coalition while saying Eritrea is not currently part of it.

The significance of Tsimdo lies not simply in whether its members share the same political programme, but in what they appear willing to put aside to cooperate.

Major disputes remain unresolved: displaced people have yet to return to some contested areas, including Welkait, while territorial claims continue to divide Tigray and Amhara actors.

Yet groups that once fought on opposing sides now appear willing to set aside some of those differences when cooperation can increase pressure on the federal government.

That raises a further question about the TPLF’s post-Pretoria strategy. The organisation appears to be rebuilding its political influence while retaining links to military structures, even as many Tigrayans remain displaced and fear renewed mobilisation.

The emerging convergence points to a potentially widening gap between the strategic calculations of political and armed actors and the immediate interests of civilians still dealing with the consequences of war.

The groups have different histories and political ambitions, and their cooperation may not last. But their willingness to find common ground against Addis Ababa matters.

For the TPLF, Tsimdo offers another arena in which to build political and strategic relationships beyond Tigray.

The war displaced about 1.9 million people. Many remain unable to return, particularly to disputed areas including Welkait, Tsegede, Humera and Raya.

Those territorial disputes remain closely tied to the return of displaced Tigrayans, while the political relationship between Tigray and the federal government remains unsettled.

The federal government has also failed to deliver on important elements of the post-war settlement. But those failures do not erase the TPLF’s commitments under Pretoria.

Article 6 envisaged the disarmament, demobilisation and reintegration of its fighters. Article 7 banned conscription, mobilisation and preparations for renewed conflict.

The record since 2024 does not prove that Pretoria was deliberately used by the TPLF to buy time.

It does, however, show a movement that has remained politically organised, fought to regain control of Tigray’s institutions, retained links to armed structures and found new potential partners as the settlement stalled.

Pretoria ended the large-scale war. It did not settle the struggle over power, territory and security that lay beneath it.

For Tigrayans, however, the calculations are simpler.

A young man from Tigray, who spoke to Al Jazeera on condition of anonymity, said: “The fear of being drafted is what’s making many youth lose hope.”

The Pretoria peace deal ended Ethiopia’s Tigray war but left political and territorial disputes unresolved, as the TPLF has sought to reassert its influence and build new strategic relationships [Getty Images] (Getty)

Ethiopia’s Tigray region remains caught between an unfinished peace process and renewed political and military tensions nearly four years after the Pretoria agreement ended the war [Yasuyoshi Chiba / AFP]

articles.title: Illinois mother charged with murder after killing 2-year-old, attempting to harm herself
articles.summary: A suburban Illinois mother, who had become interested in the Lindsay Clancy case, has been charged with murder after she allegedly killed her 2-year-old son then attempted to harm herself, according to police and court records.
articles.body: A suburban Illinois mother, who had become interested in the Lindsay Clancy case, has been charged with murder after she allegedly killed her 2-year-old son then attempted to harm herself, according to police and court records. A quiet street in the affluent village of Frankfort, Illinois, about 35 miles southwest of Chicago, became a scene of terror earlier this week when the 2-year-old child was found hanging in the basement and his mother, Corie A. Walsh, was discovered in a bathtub in an apparent suicide attempt. Walsh, 40, was charged with three counts of first-degree murder on Friday, police announced. Before the killing, Walsh had “recently become very invested in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial,” prosecutors said in their petition to deny her pretrial release. Clancy, who was accused of murdering her three children in January 2023, has been in the national spotlight the last few weeks as her trial was live-streamed. It culminated in a mistrial Friday. Walsh had been “actively discussing the case” in group text messages with her friends up until 12:30 p.m. Tuesday — just three and a half hours before the grisly scene at her home was discovered, the filing said. At the time in the trial, the jury was in deliberations. Frankfort police had responded to the home just after 4 p.m. Tuesday on a report of an unresponsive child, authorities said. When officers arrived they found a neighbor performing CPR on the toddler, Barrett Walsh, who she had found hanging in the basement, court documents said. The neighbor took the child down and attempted CPR while calling 911, but he was already cold with no pulse, prosecutors said. The child was transported to a local hospital, where he was pronounced deceased. The Will County Coroner’s Office ruled his death as an apparent homicide. Preliminary findings of the autopsy say he died from asphyxia due to ligature compression of the neck, the petition said. Officers found Walsh in the bathroom of the upstairs master bedroom, laying in a tub fully dressed and “surrounded by bloody water.” Walsh was found with cuts to her wrists and thighs, the petition said. She was taken to a hospital with non-life-threatening injuries, police said. Walsh told officers “she did this to her baby because he was the ‘devil’ and the ‘anti-Christ,’” the filing said. The neighbor told officers she had found Walsh with a knife in her hands, “actively harming herself.” The neighbor took the knife and threw it into the sink, and it was later taken into evidence, according to the petition. After she took the knife away, Walsh asked her why she did that, “as she was trying to kill herself,” the petition said. Walsh then told the neighbor that “Bear,” the child’s nickname, was “in the basement,” the filing said. Police on Wednesday said that the preliminary investigation indicated it was a domestic-related homicide. Walsh’s husband was out of town at the time. An infant was home and unharmed, prosecutors said. Two school-aged children had returned home around the time Barrett was found and they were also physically unharmed, the filing said. Walsh allegedly made statements regarding harming her other children and statements that she intended to harm her husband upon his return home, prosecutors said in the filing. Once hospitalized, she also described to officers “the manner in which she killed Barrett,” which was consistent with evidence at the scene, the petition said. Walsh was in custody Friday night and being held for medical treatment. Once released, she’ll be transferred to the Will County Adult Detention Facility. It was not immediately clear whether she has retained an attorney. Frankfort police called the case a “heartbreaking tragedy,” saying, “We ask our community to keep them in their thoughts and prayers.” If you or someone you know is struggling or in emotional distress, call or text 988, or chat at 988lifeline.org 24/7, to reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For additional resources, visit SpeakingOfSuicide.com/resources.

images.caption: Corie A. Walsh was charged with three counts of first-degree murder and is now in custody "and being held for medical treatment" after the murder of a 2-year-old child inside a Frankfort home.

articles.title: Malaysia declares emergency in Sarawak as haze from Indonesia worsens
articles.summary: Country implements state of emergency in Sarawak’s Serian district after air pollution reaches ‘hazardous’ levels.
articles.body:
Malaysia has declared a state of emergency in a district in Sarawak state after haze caused by wildfires in neighbouring Indonesia increased air pollution to “hazardous” levels.

King Sultan Ibrahim “has consented to the declaration of emergency throughout Serian Division, Sarawak, following haze conditions that have reached air pollution levels hazardous to public health and safety”, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s office said in a statement on Thursday.

The declaration followed a formal request from the Sarawak Disaster Management Committee after the region’s Air Pollutant Index reached levels warranting consideration of a local emergency.

Under the order, 647 schools in Serian will close from Monday until at least the end of next week, alongside government and private offices, plantations, construction sites and quarries, with only essential services continuing to operate.

The state’s disaster management authorities said a three-day cloud-seeding operation launched on Thursday would be extended to at least Monday, citing forecasts of “more conducive cloud formations” during that period.

Sarawak State Disaster Management Committee chairman Douglas Uggah Embas, speaking at a news conference in Kuching, stressed that the emergency applied only to Serian, not the entire state, but urged residents there to take the situation seriously .

“Please minimise outdoor activities and avoid strenuous activities outdoors,” he said.

Sarawak, in the northern part of Borneo island, has been heavily affected by haze for weeks, as have the neighbouring states of Sabah and Peninsular Malaysia.

Other Southeast Asian countries like Brunei have also reported smoggy conditions. Singapore announced it would start providing daily haze advisories from Friday evening, after the 24-hour air quality readings entered the unhealthy range, the first since 2023.

It has also hit the Philippines, where President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. ordered the suspension of classes in the capital region, Metro Manila, as well as more than a dozen provinces on Friday.

This year’s transboundary haze, which originates from fires burning across Indonesia , particularly the Kalimantan region and Sumatra island, is part of a wider seasonal wildfire crisis in the archipelago country.

Scientists say temperatures are expected to peak this month, potentially intensifying the fires by bringing hotter and drier conditions across the region.

images.caption: This aerial photo taken from a commercial plane shows haze from Indonesian forest fires blanketing a residential district in Kuching, the capital city of Sarawak state on the island of Borneo, on September 5, 2026 [Mohd Rasfan/AFP]

articles.title: Blasts at Bolivian military base kill at least 10, injure dozens
articles.summary: Authorities say seven people are still missing after deadly explosions at a facility storing pyrotechnic material.
articles.body:
Two explosions at a military facility in the Bolivian city of Viacha have killed at least 10 people and injured dozens of others, authorities said.

The blasts occurred on Friday in an area used to store pyrotechnic material, about 30km (18 miles) from the administrative capital, La Paz, Bolivia’s Ministry of Defence said.

Viacha health director Rita Nebraska told a local television station that between 10 and 15 people were believed to have been killed and 62 others were injured.

She said 14 of the wounded were transferred to hospitals in La Paz, including a girl with third-degree burns.

Fireworks were stored at the military facility, but the cause of the explosions remains under investigation, police spokesman Roger Roca said. He added that seven people were still missing.

Firefighters warned that a heat source remained at the site, Nebraska said, urging residents to stay at least 150 metres away because of the risk of another explosion.

Police said dozens of nearby homes were damaged and that many civilians were injured by shattered glass.

About 50 civilians and six military personnel injured in the explosions “have been treated … by the different medical centres of Viacha”, Deputy Minister of Defence Ernesto Justiniano Urenda said in a statement.

An investigation is under way to determine the cause of the explosions, how the pyrotechnic material was stored and whether anyone was responsible, he added.

Footage posted on social media showed one of the explosions shattering windows in nearby buildings and sending debris into the air as thick black smoke rose from the facility.

articles.title: Germany’s far-right AfD is poised for power – and split on whether to cozy up to Trump
articles.summary: The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party is speeding into state elections in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday with a sizeable lead in the polls. If the party gets an outright majority, it will mark the first time the far right has won an absolute majority in a state election since World War II.
articles.body: The Alternative for Germany (AfD) party is speeding into state elections in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday with a sizeable lead in the polls. If the party gets an outright majority, it will put the far right in charge of a state for the first time since World War II. The party is projected to get 42% of the vote in the eastern German state, according to pollster Infratest dimap – a massive jump compared to its support just a couple years ago, and potentially enough to propel it to power in the country’s electoral system. But there are roadblocks to the AfD expanding its success in mainstream German politics. The party has been classified as “extremist” by German intelligence for its rhetoric in relation to Muslim citizens of Germany and on immigration, and it’s been denounced by mainstream conservatives and progressives alike. All other parties in the country operate a so-called “firewall” – an unwritten rule to not form a coalition with the AfD or work together in parliament. If the AfD doesn’t get an absolute majority in Sunday’s elections, all other parties could form a ragtag coalition to shut it out of power in the state. It’s partly that isolation at home that has compelled the AfD to seek out ties with the United States’ MAGA movement. It’s also partly the shared right-wing politics and the brazen rhetoric and branding – hats with the slogan “Make Germany Great Again” are not uncommon at AfD events now. And the ties go well beyond merch. The party’s co-leader Alice Weidel met with US Vice President JD Vance on the sidelines of the Munch Security Conference last year. Before that, she also joined Elon Musk for a livestream event on his platform, X. And a small group of AfD politicians travelled to Washington for US President Donald Trump’s second inauguration. In return, Trump administration officials have also lent the party a hand on several occasions. Vance used his 2025 speech in Munich to urge German lawmakers to end their “firewall” against the far-right. Secretary of State Marco Rubio decried German authorities officially labelling the party as extremist, calling the decision “tyranny in disguise.” But as Trump continues to raise eyebrows in Europe for some of his foreign policy moves – particularly the war in Iran, saber-rattling in Greenland and intervention in Venezuela – some factions of the AfD now appear interested in keeping their distance. It comes as the United States’ reputation among the German public has fallen and many of Trump’s foreign policy decisions are widely disliked. A poll by Germany’s public broadcaster ARD in March found that 58% of Germans considered the attacks on Iran unjustified. And in January, another ARD poll found that 72% of the population considered the arrest of former Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro unjustified. “I think there is ideological alignment on key issues, and I think the AfD is also learning from the MAGA movement,” said Almut Möller, the director for European and global affairs at the European Policy Centre, a think tank in Brussels. The two parties particularly align when it comes to rhetoric about how the country should “care about (its) own people and stop caring about everybody else,” Möller said. “Having said that, it is not a straightforward relationship to handle at all times,” Möller told CNN, particularly when it comes to “policies that affect the German economy,” such as the Trump tariffs or pain at the gas pump amid the Iran war. Against that backdrop, the leaders of the AfD have yo-yoed back and forth between praising Trump’s domestic stances on immigration, culture war issues and nationalism, while criticizing his interference in other countries. ‘It would be weird if Trump would protect German interests’ The AfD lawmaker who also serves as the party’s foreign policy spokesperson, Markus Frohnmaier, told CNN he has made multiple trips to the United States this year and has fostered strong links with the MAGA movement. Speaking in his office in the Bundestag just days before the election, he said their politics have plenty in common, especially on the issue of immigration. The AfD has campaigned on proposals to deport migrants and refugees, as well as expand mass detention facilities – a policy widely referred to as “remigration.” Party officials have frequently used anti-Muslim rhetoric and singled out Muslim and Ukrainian residents when talking about who they wish to deport. Another pledge is to create separate schools for the children of refugees, to teach them the curriculum of their home countries. With a US border patrol cap displayed on his bookcase, Frohnmaier called Trump’s handling of migration “really impressive,” adding, “I think this is something what we need in Germany too – a really good border control, probably something like ICE, and that would improve the situation dramatically.” Frohnmaier also has in his office a famous 2020 photo of Trump holding a bible at a Washington, DC, church amid protests near the White House. But Frohnmaier was clear that there are American policies he doesn’t support. “My colleagues and friends in the US know that we are more critical when it comes to the war in Iran,” he said. When it comes to the hot-button issue of US tariffs, Frohnmaier said, “I mean, it would be a bit weird if Donald Trump would protect German interests, right?” “It’s okay to agree not in all points with each other… They need to protect American interests, and we’re German, and we try to protect our interests,” he told CNN. Frohnmaier, who has also made multiple trips to Russia, has walked a careful tightrope in his foreign policy role – courting MAGA Republicans at the same time as establishing ties with Kremlin insiders. ‘We see American interests, we see Russian interests’ For supposedly a state-level election, Russia has been a feature. “We’re quite transparent about saying that we want an especially good relationship with Russia, of course, but also with the United States of America, because those are simply important players in this world,” said Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD candidate for the premiership in Saxony-Anhalt, who would lead the state in the event that his party gets an outright majority of votes on Sunday. “We see American interests, we see Russian interests, but we have our own interest, namely the German interest,” Siegmund told CNN in an August interview. The AfD’s support of Russia is no secret – the party is against further aid and defense packages for Ukraine, often referring to defense funding for Kyiv as money that is not being spent on programs for German people. Key party officials have also made frequent trips to Moscow, St. Petersberg and the occupied Crimean peninsula – something that has raised alarm bells among corruption watchdogs. The AfD has also vowed to bring back the cheap Russian gas that once fueled Germany but has been phased out following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. But for eastern states, like Saxony-Anhalt, which were once under the purview of the Soviet Union, Möller said “it runs deeper than the cost of energy. There is a long tradition of working with Russia in Germany.” Culture wars coming to Germany Of course, issues of foreign relations and immigration aren’t decided on the state level. Analyst Grégoire Roos, the director of the Europe and Russia and Eurasia Programs at Chatham House, said he would expect the AfD to lean more into issues of culture, education and local policing if it secures power in Saxony-Anhalt. “You would likely see patterns comparable to those we’ve seen in the US in terms of how you change school programs, put pressure on police forces,” Roos told CNN. Roos also said he would expect to see the AfD state government take up “cultural fights” such as banning LGBTQ+ flags, restricting inclusion policies in schools, creating rules to raise the German flag in schools and possibly enacting changes in history books. “I think those would not transform daily life, as such, but it would infringe on some of some of what is seen as basic liberties in Germany,” the analyst said. “They will understand that this is a laboratory, a window to or magnifying glass put on what they could deliver at a national scale, and so they would focus on symbols.” A win would also give the AfD a presence in Germany’s upper house of parliament, the Bundesrat, which would be a symbolic win for the party, but would likely not move the needle much on national policy. “This is of course a strong opportunity to basically show that they’re at the gates of power now,” Möller added. “Even though Saxony-Anhalt is a small federal state and has less than 2 million inhabitants, this will resonate more widely.” The polls indicate the election could go either way. All other mainstream parties in Saxony-Anhalt are polling at 54% combined, according to Infratest dimap. Some of those parties won’t even reach the 5% threshold to have any of their votes counted, which is why the AfD could secure power with less than half the electorate. Taken together, it means the AfD’s projected support of 42% presents a loud knock on those gates of power.
